summary: This standards-track memo defines a negative acknowledgement mechanism for Signaling Compression (SigComp). When a compressed message cannot be decompressed, the receiver can report precise error information, which the sender can use to adjust its compression.

plainLanguage.summary: If you cannot understand a message, you tell the sender exactly what went wrong. This lets compressed messages be fixed or resent more cleverly.

questions: what happens when sigcomp decompression fails
subtitle: How a SigComp receiver tells the sender exactly why a compressed message could not be decompressed.

tldr.problem: SigComp senders and receivers can disagree about what compression state is stored, because of discarded compartments, client restarts or server failover. Existing recovery needed a reverse-direction message that might never be sent.
tldr.mechanism: When a message cannot be decompressed, the receiver sends a NACK. It is a valid SigComp message carrying a reason code, the failed opcode and program counter, the SHA-1 hash of the failed message and optional error details.
tldr.outcome: The sender finds the message by its hash and adjusts the compressor for the right compartment, for example by dropping a missing state or sending uncompressed. Implementations that send NACKs advertise SigComp version 0x02.

today: RFC 4077 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends SigComp as defined in RFC 3320.

sections.title: Why SigComp Needs a NACK
sections.content:
Signaling Compression (SigComp, RFC 3320) carries compressed messages between two network elements. A sender can ask the receiver to store state objects for later reuse. RFC 3321 lets a sender confirm that state was created, but operational experience showed that the sender's and receiver's views of shared state can still differ.

The RFC names three causes:

  • Compartment disposal. State is kept in compartments, which represent one instance of a remote application. Stuck compartments must eventually be discarded, and discarding without explicit signaling can remove an active one.
  • Client restart. SigComp was motivated by compression over radio links, so one endpoint is often a mobile unit. A restart, for example from a battery running out, leaves the server believing the client holds state it no longer has.
  • Server failover. With DNS SRV lookup, traffic to a failed server goes to an equivalent server that resolves to the same compartment but lacks the state. Replicating state needs a two-phase commit that adds complexity and can hurt performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people use a shared codebook, but one of them lost a page without knowing. They keep writing in code the other cannot read.

sections.title: The Solution in Brief
sections.content:
SigComp can already signal that all state is lost by setting state_memory_size to 0 in one message in the reverse direction. The RFC calls that incomplete: it wipes out a whole compartment when only one state is bad, and it needs a reverse message that the remote application will authorize. In pure client/server deployments such a message may never be sent.

The proposed fix is a simple Negative Acknowledgement (NACK). It carries a reason code for the failure and, for some failures, extra details that help recovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Rather than throwing away the whole codebook, the receiver just says which page is missing.

sections.title: How Nodes Send and Handle NACKs
sections.content:
A sender that uses NACKs calculates and stores a SHA-1 hash of each SigComp message it sends, in a way that lets it find the compartment that message belonged to.

When a received message fails to decompress, the recipient sends a NACK holding the SHA-1 hash of that message, the exact reason and any helpful details. Over a connection-oriented transport such as TCP, the NACK goes back on the same connection, and the standard SigComp delimiter 0xFFFF ends it on a stream. Over a connectionless transport such as UDP, it goes to the IP address and port the message came from, sent from the address and port the bad message was sent to.

On receiving a NACK, the node uses the 20-byte SHA-1 hash to find the original message and its compartment. What happens next depends on the transport:

  • Unreliable transport: the compressor for that compartment is adjusted, for example by removing the state the peer cannot retrieve. The SigComp layer must not retransmit the original message. The next application-initiated message benefits from the adjustment.
  • Reliable transport: the SigComp layer must tell the application an error occurred, and the application should react as it would to any transport error such as a TCP connection reset. The compressor is adjusted as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver points at the exact message it could not read by quoting its fingerprint. The sender then changes how it writes and, if needed, tries again.

sections.title: Detecting NACK Support
sections.content:
Knowing the peer supports NACKs is useful. Normally a sender must wait for acknowledgment of state before referencing it, which hurts compression when several messages are in flight. If the receiver supports NACKs, the sender can optimistically assume state was created and recover by NACK if that proves false, for example after packet loss or reordering.

An implementation that sends NACKs indicates a SigComp version number of 0x02 in its Universal Decompressor Virtual Machine (UDVM). Bytecodes sent to it can check the version and report back as requested feedback. Apart from NACK, version 0x02 behaves exactly like version 0x01.
sections.plainLanguage: If you know your friend will tell you when they are confused, you can write faster and fix mistakes later.

sections.title: The NACK Message Format
sections.content:
A NACK is a syntactically valid SigComp message designed to be safely ignored by implementations that do not support NACKs. It uses the second message variant (normally for code upload) with code_len of zero. The NACK data sits in the area normally used for input data, and the destination field serves as the NACK version, which this document defines as 1.

  • Reason Code: one byte saying what failed.
  • OPCODE of failed instruction: one byte, 0 if failure came before the UDVM ran any code.
  • PC of failed instruction: two bytes, most significant byte first, also 0 if the UDVM had not started.
  • SHA-1 Hash of failed message: the full 20 bytes, computed over the whole SigComp message from the header byte to the end of the input. Lower-level headers and the 0xFFFF delimiter are excluded, and 0xFFxx escapes are un-escaped first on stream transports.
  • Error Details: extra information whose meaning depends on the reason code.
sections.plainLanguage: The note says what went wrong, where in the instructions it happened, and the fingerprint of the message that caused it.

sections.title: Reason Codes
sections.content:
The RFC defines 25 reason codes. Many are mainly useful for debugging interoperability. STATE_NOT_FOUND is the notable exception, because it generally makes the recipient encode future messages without the indicated state. For other codes, an implementation would typically use different bytecodes or send that message uncompressed.

Only five codes carry details: STATE_NOT_FOUND and ID_NOT_UNIQUE and STATE_TOO_SHORT give a state ID of 6 to 20 bytes, CYCLES_EXHAUSTED gives cycles per bit in one byte, and BYTECODES_TOO_LARGE gives the receiver's decompression memory size in two bytes. For all other codes the details field has zero length.

For STATE_TOO_SHORT, implementers are cautioned to return only the partial state identifier that was requested, because extra identifier bytes could help an attacker access the state. For FRAMING_ERROR, a hash cannot be determined, so the hash field should be all zeros.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has a numbered list of reasons, like a teacher marking exactly which kind of mistake you made.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Two issues are discussed. For reflector attacks, an attacker could trigger NACKs by sending malformed messages with a spoofed IP address. But each bad message produces only one NACK, and NACKs are small, so there is no amplification. The RFC adds that nearly all deployed protocols behave the same way.

For NACK spoofing, forged NACKs are possible but do little harm. Reporting lost state usually just causes the state to be re-sent, and other codes lead to an alternate compression method or uncompressed messages. These make messages slightly larger, with no catastrophic security implications.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could fake a complaint note, but all it makes you do is write a little more plainly for a while.

items.label: Header
items.desc: Bits 11111, a T bit, then 0, as in a normal SigComp message.

items.label: Returned feedback item
items.desc: Feedback item returned as in SigComp.

items.label: code_len = 0 and version = 1
items.desc: Marks the message as a NACK of version 1.

items.label: Reason Code
items.desc: Nature of the decompression failure.

items.label: OPCODE of failed instruction
items.desc: 0 if failure came before any code ran.

items.label: PC of failed instruction
items.desc: Program counter, big endian.

items.label: SHA-1 Hash of failed message
items.desc: Identifies the message that could not be decompressed.

items.label: Error Details
items.desc: Depends on the reason code; may be empty.

items.label: STATE_NOT_FOUND
items.desc: Referenced state cannot be found; details give the state ID (6 - 20 bytes).

items.label: CYCLES_EXHAUSTED
items.desc: Decompression used more cycles than allocated; details give cycles per bit.

items.label: USER_REQUESTED
items.desc: The DECOMPRESSION-FAILURE opcode was executed.

items.label: SEGFAULT
items.desc: Access outside the UDVM memory space.

items.label: TOO_MANY_STATE_REQUESTS
items.desc: More than four state store or delete requests.

items.label: INVALID_STATE_ID_LENGTH
items.desc: State ID length below 6 or above 20.

items.label: OUTPUT_OVERFLOW
items.desc: Decompressed message too large for the receiver.

items.label: DIV_BY_ZERO
items.desc: DIVIDE or REMAINDER with a divisor of 0.

items.label: MESSAGE_TOO_SHORT
items.desc: Not enough bytes for a valid SigComp message.

items.label: BYTECODES_TOO_LARGE
items.desc: Uploaded bytecodes exceed UDVM memory; details give memory size (2 bytes).

items.label: ID_NOT_UNIQUE
items.desc: A partial state identifier matched more than one state item.

items.label: STATE_TOO_SHORT
items.desc: STATE-ACCESS tried to copy more bytes than the state holds.

items.label: FRAMING_ERROR
items.desc: Framing error on a stream transport; hash field all zeros.
